verdicts.trueWording: AI's tendency to hallucinate regarding places or events that don't already
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext (action=raw) of Wikivoyage:Votes for deletion/September 2025, section 'Articles created by A Sulaiman Z'. SelfieCity, 11:59, 22 August 2025 (UTC), votes Delete; the quoted clause runs on to 'have an online presence' and he then says he suspects much of the content in those articles is false. The listed pages are Nigerian localities (Birniwa, Dawakin Kudu, Katagum and about two dozen more); the page calls them articles or African destinations rather than 'towns', though the descriptor is accurate. SelfieCity is the second commenter, so 'another editor' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: see the ChatGPT-ish bulleted list at the end of the article
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext of Wikivoyage:Votes for deletion/January 2025. SelfieCity, 20:53, 2 January 2025 (UTC), opens the section headed '[[Ambler (Alaska)]]' - so this is the nomination - saying the article appears AI-written, citing the quoted list as an example, and proposing deletion. Ambler is an Alaskan town. Mild softening: the list is offered as one example ('For example'), not stated as the sole ground.

verdicts.trueWording: I am surprised we don't have any AI rules
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext of Wikivoyage:Travellers' pub, section 'AI guidelines'. Signed Sgroey, 02:12, 2 September 2026 (UTC), so 'as of September 2026' holds. The en.wikivoyage user-rights API gives Sgroey groups autopatrolled/user - an ordinary editor. The page nowhere states Sgroey's gender, so the pronoun 'he' is not evidenced by the source.

verdicts.trueWording: if an article is mostly visibly AI-generated
verdicts.note: Same section: SHB2000, 02:53, 3 September 2026 (UTC), replies to Sgroey that this is mostly true but that a WV:CSD speedy-deletion provision exists, in the quoted terms. The pub page does not itself call SHB2000 an administrator; the en.wikivoyage user-rights API returns groups bureaucrat, checkuser and sysop for that account, which confirms the 'administrator' limb from the same site's records.

verdicts.trueWording: the model texts remained less diverse, more affectively positive
verdicts.note: arxiv.org/html/2604.20048v3, 'Culturally uneven urban perception in large language models', first author Rong Zhao; the abs page's submission history dates v3 to 8 June 2026, matching the citation. The sentence closes the UK Geograph results paragraph and states the comparison is against the human benchmark, so the 'than the human benchmark' limb is explicit.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'identity-perception indices' - the paper's IPI is the sentiment-based ingroup preference index, not an identity-perception index
verdicts.trueWording: the model estimates were systematically more elevated
verdicts.note: Same paragraph of arXiv 2604.20048v3: human texts gave negative IPIs for all three nations (-0.400 England, -0.256 Scotland, -0.062 Wales) on the 270-image nation-labelled Geograph subset, and the quoted clause follows, adding that several model estimates were positive (Fig. 3e). The quote is verbatim and the numeric substance holds; only the expansion of the acronym is wrong - Fig. 2c defines IPI as the sentiment-based ingroup preference index.

NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks PDF fetched and extracted with pdftotext -layout. Table 1 on p.7 carries the row; the seven 4-choice figures are 39.0, 35.6, 46.0, 44.7, 39.5, 40.8 and 33.6, so 46.0 is the best of the seven, and the caption says bold marks the best-performing model. The abstract independently gives 46% for GPT-4-Turbo and describes the test as graduate-level. The table spells the model 'GPT-4-turbo'.

Same Table 1, p.7: 33.6 is the lowest 4-choice balanced accuracy among the seven models, and the abstract states the range as running from 33.6% for Llama-3.1-8B up to 46% for GPT-4-Turbo, so the 'weakest model tested' limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: random guessing (25%) but falling short of expert comprehension
verdicts.note: Abstract of the HiST-LLM paper, immediately after the 33.6-46% range, preceded by 'outperforming'. The same finding is restated in the Introduction and again in the Conclusion, where the models are said to beat random guessing while falling short of comprehensive expert-level knowledge.

verdicts.trueWording: achieves 55.3% for 8,000-6,000 BCE, drops to 38.7% for 1,500-2,000 CE
verdicts.note: The claim carried no quote, so it is graded on substance. The prose immediately below Table 2 (p.8) gives exactly this example for GPT-4-Turbo, naming both periods and both figures, and Table 2's rows confirm 55.3 [48.0, 62.5] for the 8k-6k BCE bin and 38.7 [37.4, 40.0] for the 1.5k-2k CE bin. Both numbers, both period labels and the direction of the fall match.

Introduction, p.2: the sentence begins 'All variables' and continues with the quoted words, so the 'every Seshat variable carries that marking' limb is supported. The same section states that the benchmark's questions also explicitly ask whether a fact is evidenced or inferred from indirect evidence, supporting the other limb. Location correction: the passage sits in Section 1 (Introduction), not Section 3; the page number p.2 is right.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the attributed byline - the TechCrunch piece is bylined Charles Rollet, not Kyle Wiggers
verdicts.note: Live page fetched with a browser user agent. The third body paragraph names GPT-4 Turbo as the best-performing LLM and carries the quoted words, adding that this is not much higher than random guessing. Dateline 7:01 AM PST, January 19, 2025, matches the cited date; the headline and Hist-LLM/Seshat framing match. Every limb of the claim sentence holds - only the author in the source line is wrong.

verdicts.trueWording: History is often viewed as facts, but sometimes interpretation is necessary
verdicts.note: Complexity Science Hub news page, dated 21.01.2025, fetched live. The quoted words are attributed to del Rio-Chanona and continue 'to make sense of it'; she is described there as a CSH external faculty member and a UCL assistant professor, and as the study's corresponding author.

verdicts.trueWording: human summaries scored 61 (81%) and the Gen AI summaries
verdicts.note: aph.gov.au DocumentStore PDF fetched (1.99 MB, PDF 1.7) and text-extracted. Section 6 DISCUSSION of the attached AWS report states the maximum was 75 points and carries the quoted words, with the Gen AI figure 35 (47%). ASIC's own answer text uses 'aggregated' of both sets and repeats the same two scores, so the 'aggregated' and 'of 75' limbs both hold.

verdicts.trueWording: AI summaries performed lower on all criteria
verdicts.note: Same PDF, ASIC's answer to Question on Notice No. 001 (before the attached AWS report, p.2 of the answer): the final results are reported in the quoted terms, compared with the human summaries. The discussion section repeats that the Gen AI summaries scored lower on all criteria. Header block confirms the Select Committee on Adopting Artificial Intelligence, Question No. 001, reference 21 May 2024.
